skills.name: Growth of firms: mergers, takeovers and integration

note.text: External growth combines existing businesses through arrangements such as mergers or takeovers. Horizontal integration links firms at the same stage in the same industry. Vertical integration links different stages: backward towards inputs, forward towards customers. Conglomerate integration combines unrelated activities in the classroom model. Merger and takeover describe how businesses combine or control changes, while horizontal and vertical describe their relationship. Potential savings, supply security or diversification must be weighed against integration costs, financing risk and reduced competition.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to classify external growth by the firms’ relationship and evaluate a possible gain against a risk. Builds on: internal growth and the benefits and limits of scale. Leads to: why some firms remain small and how growth changes location needs.

sections.heading: Understand the economics
sections.text: External growth combines existing businesses through arrangements such as mergers or takeovers. Horizontal integration links firms at the same stage in the same industry. Vertical integration links different stages: backward towards inputs, forward towards customers. Conglomerate integration combines unrelated activities in the classroom model. Merger and takeover describe how businesses combine or control changes, while horizontal and vertical describe their relationship. Potential savings, supply security or diversification must be weighed against integration costs, financing risk and reduced competition.

sections.heading: Follow the local case
sections.text: A fictional bakery buying a flour supplier differs from buying another bakery or a retail outlet. The first can improve coordination with supply, but ownership does not guarantee low input costs. Combining rivals can reduce competition even if the managers also expect savings. None of these examples announces a real acquisition.

sections.heading: Reason and check
sections.text: Draw the production chain before choosing forward or backward. State both a plausible mechanism of benefit and a possible disadvantage. Do not assume combining firms automatically adds their profits without transition costs or that diversification eliminates every risk.

cards.idea: Distinguish these features before judging a business.
example: horizontal integration: combining firms at the same stage in the same industry.
backward integration: extending control towards an earlier input-supply stage.
forward integration: extending control towards distribution or final customers.
conglomerate integration: combining unrelated activities in the stated model.

cards.idea: Use the stated case evidence to identify the economic feature.
example: Two fictional bakeries combine their businesses.
The fictional bakery acquires its flour supplier.
The bakery acquires retail outlets selling its bread.
The bakery combines with an unrelated furniture maker.

cards.idea: Explain a consequence instead of assuming every option has the same effect.
example: horizontal integration: The firms must share the industry and production stage in this classification.
backward integration: An input supplier is upstream, so the direction is backward.
forward integration: Retail lies closer to final customers than the bakery’s production stage.
conglomerate integration: Different activities can spread exposure but still involve shared finance and management risks.
